$comment: Shape contract for a project's mcp.manifest.json. The verdict that gates epic close comes from checkManifest() in factory/orchestrator/src/mcp.ts, which reports stable rule ids (MCP-P1, MCP-T4, ...) from the numbered baseline in docs/standards/mcp.md; this schema is the shape half of the same contract and its descriptions name the rule each field serves. Rules that are not decidable from a declaration (MCP-P3 session independence, MCP-S1 output redaction, MCP-X5 state-handle binding, MCP-X6 SSRF blocks) are enforced in code, not here.
title: MCP Manifest
description: The single declaration of what a project's MCP surface exposes: its identity, its wire revision, its transport, and every tool with its mutation class, annotations, and operator sign-off. This file is the one place an operator reads to know what an agent can do with this project.

name.description: MCP-P2. Server identity as reported in the initialize result; conventionally the project name.

version.description: MCP-P2. Semver. A client caches a tool surface against this, so bump it when the surface changes.

protocolRevision.description: MCP-P1. The pinned wire revision — what the Tier-1 TypeScript SDK actually negotiates, not the newest revision on paper. Moves to 2026-07-28 when the SDK ships it; see docs/standards/mcp.md 'Forward compatibility'.

tools.description: MCP-T5. Every tool the server registers, and nothing it does not. A server that can do more than this array admits makes the manifest a lie.

transport.description: MCP-X1. stdio is the default and opens no port; http is a deliberate opt-in that must carry its own preconditions.

cloudflareAccess.description: MCP-X2 (mcp.md). Cloudflare Access in front: nothing is exposed beyond localhost without something authenticating for it.

resourceServer.description: MCP-X3/X4. The server is an OAuth 2.0 protected resource, and says so precisely enough to be checkable.

canonicalUri.description: MCP-X3. The canonical resource URI. This is the token audience — every accepted token must name it.

authorizationServers.description: MCP-X3. Issuers this resource trusts. Validate the returned `iss` against these (RFC 9207) to close the mix-up attack.

resourceIndicators.description: MCP-X3. RFC 8707 resource indicators are mandatory: they are what binds an issued token to this server rather than to whoever asks next.

tokenPassthrough.description: MCP-X4. Never allowed. The server MUST NOT accept any token that was not explicitly issued for it.

scopes.description: Least privilege. Wildcards ('*', 'all', 'full-access') defeat the point of asking.

name.description: MCP-T5. snake_case, unique within the manifest. This is what an agent types.

title.description: Human-facing label, shown in consent prompts.

description.description: What the tool does, written for the agent deciding whether to call it.

mutation.description: MCP-T2. What this tool actually does to the world. read-only is the default and the only class that needs no sign-off. The implementation passes this same class to requireDeclaredTool(), so a tool that quietly starts writing fails to boot instead of shipping under its old declaration.

annotations.description: MCP-T1/T2/T3. The hints an agent reads to decide whether a call is safe. They must agree with `mutation` — a read-only tool with destructiveHint true is a contradiction, not a nuance.

openWorldHint.description: MCP-T3. True when the tool reaches something outside this project's own state. Every outbound tool sets it.

approval.description: MCP-T4. Operator sign-off, required for every tool that is not read-only. A person decided, at the mcp surface milestone, that an agent may do this unattended.

allOf.$comment: MCP-T1. read-only implies its own annotations.
MCP-T4. Anything that is not read-only carries a sign-off.
MCP-T2. A mutating tool must not advertise itself as safe.
MCP-T3. outbound reaches beyond this project.
